title: Indus Valley Civilisation
deck: How planned cities, standard bricks and carved seals appeared on the Indus plains — and why the cities faded.
confidenceNote: Medium — dating of phases is debated

chapters.heading: Rivers and first villages
chapters.body: The story starts before the cities. Farming communities settled the Indus and Ghaggar-Hakra basins, and sites such as Mehrgarh show settled life in the region thousands of years earlier.

chapters.heading: The cities appear
chapters.body: By about 2600 BCE, towns such as Harappa and Mohenjo-daro had grown into planned cities, with gridded streets, standardised baked bricks and covered drains.

chapters.heading: Trade, seals and weights
chapters.body: Craftspeople made stamp seals, beads and standardised weights. Seals and goods found in Mesopotamia point to long-distance trade.

chapters.heading: A script no one can read
chapters.body: Short inscriptions on seals and pottery remain undeciphered, so much of what we know comes from archaeology rather than from written records.

chapters.heading: Decline
chapters.body: From about 1900 BCE the big cities declined and people spread to smaller settlements. Shifting rivers and changing monsoons are often discussed, but the causes are still debated.

keyIdea.text: Many Indus cities share the same brick proportions and weight standards, which suggests a high degree of coordination across a very large area.
